headline: Healey faces bond-market scrutiny as Budget arrives on Wednesday 28 October

terms.meaning: Bonds the UK government sells to borrow money.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the official body that checks the government's sums.
Limits the government sets itself on how much it can borrow.

levels.headline: Healey faces bond-market scrutiny as Budget arrives on Wednesday 28 October
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver the Budget on Wednesday 28 October, with the government saying it is built on fiscal discipline and will move power and money out of Westminster.
The backdrop is difficult. Sticky inflation, high borrowing costs and weak growth leave little room for manoeuvre. The 10-year gilt yield has been around 5.35% to 5.44%, close to its highest since 2007, and the 30-year yield topped 6% earlier this month. Mr Healey wants a fiscal buffer against uncertainty.
The Office for Budget Responsibility will publish new forecasts alongside the Budget. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Mr Healey have not yet set out the full mix of tax rises or savings needed to meet the fiscal rules. Euronews reports that bank bosses were summoned to a meeting, fuelling speculation about bank taxes, but nothing is confirmed.
levels.why: The Budget will set taxes and spending, and bond investors will judge whether the government's plans add up.

levels.headline: Healey's Budget on 28 October will be judged by the gilt market
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, presents his Budget on Wednesday 28 October. Ministers describe it as a Budget of fiscal discipline that pushes power and money out of Westminster.
Gilt markets are the main constraint. The 10-year yield sits near 5.4%, around its highest since 2007, and 30-year yields went above 6% earlier in October. Inflation is sticky and growth is weak, so Mr Healey wants a buffer against uncertainty and must stay inside the government's fiscal rules.
The OBR will publish updated forecasts on the day. Neither the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, nor the Chancellor has detailed the tax rises or savings required. Reports that bank chiefs were summoned have led to talk of new bank taxes, which remains unconfirmed.
levels.why: Borrowing costs affect mortgages, public spending and taxes for years.

levels.headline: Chancellor prepares Budget amid high borrowing costs and market pressure
levels.body:
John Healey, the Chancellor, will deliver his Budget on Wednesday 28 October. The government says it will be disciplined and will shift money and decision-making away from Westminster.
The difficulty is the cost of government borrowing. The yield on 10-year gilts is around 5.4%, near a multi-year high, and 30-year yields briefly went above 6%. With inflation stubborn and growth weak, Mr Healey says he wants a buffer to cope with shocks.
Official forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility come out alongside it. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, and the Chancellor have not said exactly which taxes will rise. There is speculation about bank taxes after bank bosses were called to a meeting, but that is not confirmed.
levels.why: Where taxes and borrowing end up shapes living costs for households and firms.

levels.headline: Budget on Wednesday: what the Chancellor must balance
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, will present the Budget on Wednesday 28 October. The government calls it a Budget of fiscal discipline that moves power and money out of Westminster.
He faces a tough balancing act. Investors who lend to the government by buying gilts are demanding high returns: about 5.4% on 10-year bonds, close to the highest since 2007. Inflation is sticky and the economy is growing slowly, so he wants a cushion against nasty surprises.
The independent Office for Budget Responsibility will publish new forecasts. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Mr Healey have not yet explained how they will fund extra spending within their borrowing rules. Some reports suggest bank taxes, but this is only speculation.
levels.why: The decisions affect taxes, public services and the cost of borrowing.

levels.headline: Chancellor to deliver Budget as the cost of government borrowing stays high
levels.body:
On Wednesday 28 October, Chancellor John Healey will deliver the Budget. Ministers say it will be careful with money and will move power and funding out of London.
The government has to borrow, and it does so by selling bonds called gilts. Investors are asking for a high return at the moment, about 5.4% a year on 10-year gilts, which is close to the highest level since 2007. With prices still rising and growth slow, Mr Healey says he wants a safety buffer.
An official watchdog, the OBR, will publish its forecasts on the same day. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has not yet said which taxes might change. People are talking about new taxes on banks, but nothing has been confirmed.
levels.why: Government borrowing costs can feed through to mortgages and to taxes.

levels.headline: The Chancellor's Budget is on Wednesday, and borrowing is costly
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, will announce the Budget on Wednesday 28 October. This is when the government sets out how it will raise and spend money. He says it will be careful and will move money and power away from Westminster.
The government borrows by selling bonds called gilts. Right now it has to pay a high rate of interest, about 5.4% on a 10-year gilt. That is near the highest in almost twenty years. Prices are still rising quickly and the economy is growing slowly, so there is less room to spend.
An independent group called the OBR will publish its forecasts too. Nobody has said yet which taxes will change. Some people think banks may be taxed more, but that is only talk.
levels.why: The Budget affects what people pay in tax and what services get funded.

levels.headline: Budget day is Wednesday, and the government must be careful with money
levels.body:
The Chancellor is a minister who looks after the country's money. His name is John Healey. On Wednesday 28 October he will give a speech called the Budget. It says how the government plans to raise money and spend it.
The government often borrows money, a bit like taking out a loan. It does this by selling bonds called gilts. Right now it has to pay lots of interest on them, around 5.4% a year. That is high, so the Chancellor wants to be careful.
An independent team called the OBR will share its own predictions. We do not yet know what will change. Some people guess that banks might pay more tax, but nobody has said so for sure.
levels.why: A Budget changes what people pay in tax and what the government can do.

levels.headline: The Chancellor will share the Budget on Wednesday
levels.body:
Every year the government decides how to raise and spend money. The Chancellor tells everyone the plan in a speech called the Budget. This year the Chancellor is John Healey. His speech is on Wednesday 28 October.
The government sometimes borrows money. It is a bit like a family taking a loan. Right now the loan costs a lot of interest, about 5.4% each year. That is one of the highest rates for a long time. So the government has to be careful.
A group of experts called the OBR will also give their predictions. We do not know yet if any taxes will change. Some people think banks may have to pay more, but that is only a guess.
levels.why: It decides how much tax people pay and how much the government can spend.

levels.headline: Budget day: how the government plans its money
levels.body:
On Wednesday the Chancellor will give a talk about money. His name is John Healey. The talk is called the Budget. It says how much the government will take in taxes and how much it will spend on things like schools and hospitals.
The government has to borrow money, just like you might borrow a pencil from a friend and give it back later. But borrowing costs a lot right now. The government has to pay extra, called interest, about 5.4 pence for every one hundred pence each year.
Some experts will check the plan to see if the sums are right. We do not know what the Chancellor will say yet. We will find out on Wednesday.
levels.why: The Budget affects the money the government can spend on schools, hospitals and more.

levels.headline: A big money plan for the country is coming on Wednesday
levels.body:
Think of the country like a big family with a pot of money. Grown-ups called the government need to decide how to fill the pot and what to spend it on. The person in charge of the pot is the Chancellor. His name is John Healey.
On Wednesday he will tell everyone his plan. It is called the Budget. The pot pays for things like schools, hospitals and roads. Sometimes the family has to borrow money, and right now borrowing costs more than usual, like paying extra pocket money back.
A team of experts will check that the sums add up. Nobody knows the plan yet. People will listen carefully on Wednesday to find out.
levels.why: It decides how the country's money is used for things we all share.

headline: Wall Street closes lower as S&P 500 slips 0.52% on oil and AI worries

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 large US companies.
A measure of how nervous investors are about swings in the market.
An index dominated by technology companies.

levels.headline: Wall Street closes lower as S&P 500 slips 0.52% on oil and AI worries
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on Friday 23 October, the last completed session, falling 0.52% to 7,623.68. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.23%, or 652.82 points, to 52,215.16, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.21% to 25,955.34.
The Dow's slide came as US oil topped $100 a barrel amid fears that the US-Iran conflict could flare up again. Concerns about artificial intelligence spending also weighed on shares. Alphabet fell 6% ahead of its third-quarter results next week, and the Cboe Volatility Index rose 6% to 20.24.
On the week, CNBC reports the S&P 500 lost 0.5% and the Nasdaq shed 0.7%, while the Dow gained 0.4%. Other data providers calculate the weekly changes differently.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions, savings and how confident businesses feel.

levels.headline: US stocks end lower: S&P 500 down 0.52% at 7,623.68
levels.body:
US shares closed lower on Friday 23 October, the latest completed session. The S&P 500 fell 0.52% to 7,623.68, the Dow lost 1.23% (652.82 points) to 52,215.16, and the Nasdaq Composite eased 0.21% to 25,955.34.
Two themes drove the day. US crude passed $100 a barrel as investors worried that the US-Iran conflict may escalate, and doubts over AI spending continued, with Alphabet down 6% before its third-quarter earnings next week. The Cboe Volatility Index, a gauge of market anxiety, rose 6% to 20.24.
For the week, CNBC says the S&P 500 fell 0.5%, the Nasdaq 0.7% and the Dow rose 0.4%.
levels.why: Falling markets can hit pension pots and investment confidence.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes down 0.52% as oil prices and AI doubts weigh
levels.body:
The S&P 500 index of big US companies ended Friday 23 October down 0.52% at 7,623.68. This was the most recent full trading day. The Dow Jones fell 1.23% to 52,215.16, losing 652.82 points, and the Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.21% to 25,955.34.
Oil was a big factor. US crude rose above $100 a barrel on fears the conflict between the US and Iran could return. Worries about the cost of building artificial intelligence also hurt, and Alphabet dropped 6% before it reports quarterly results next week.
A measure of investor nervousness, the VIX, rose 6% to 20.24. Over the week, the S&P 500 was down 0.5%.
levels.why: Market moves reflect how worried investors are and can affect savings.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends the week lower as oil and AI fears bite
levels.body:
Shares in the United States closed lower on Friday 23 October, the last full trading day. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big US firms, fell 0.52% to 7,623.68. The Dow dropped 1.23% to 52,215.16 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq slipped 0.21% to 25,955.34.

Over the whole week the S&P 500 lost about 0.5%, according to CNBC.
levels.why: Falling share prices can reduce the value of pensions and savings.

levels.headline: US shares fall on Friday as oil tops $100 and AI worries grow

On Friday 23 October, the latest trading day that has finished, US shares ended lower. The S&P 500, a list of 500 large companies, fell 0.52% to 7,623.68. The Dow fell 1.23% to 52,215.16, and the Nasdaq, full of tech firms, fell 0.21% to 25,955.34.

levels.headline: US shares end the week lower because of oil prices and AI doubts

levels.headline: The US stock market ended lower on Friday

The stock market is a place where people buy and sell small pieces of companies, called shares. On Friday 23 October it ended lower in the United States. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big companies, fell by 0.52% to 7,623.68. The Dow fell 1.23% and the Nasdaq fell 0.21%.

levels.headline: US shares went down on Friday, and here is why

levels.headline: Share prices dipped in America on Friday

A share is a tiny piece of a company. People buy and sell them. On Friday 23 October, share prices in America dipped. A list of 500 big companies, called the S&P 500, went down by a little bit, about 0.5%. Another list, the Dow, went down by more, about 1.2%.

Prices go up and down all the time.

levels.headline: Prices of shares went down a little on Friday

Imagine a school fair where kids swap cards. If lots of kids want to sell and fewer want to buy, the price of a card drops. Something like that happened with shares on Friday 23 October. Shares are tiny pieces of companies, and their prices went down in America.
One list of 500 big companies, called the S&P 500, fell by about half of one per cent. Oil also got dearer, which can make grown-ups worried about costs. Some firms are spending lots on new computer brains, called AI, and people are not sure it will work out.
Prices go up and down. This was a small dip.
levels.why: Lots of grown-ups save money in shares, so price changes can matter to families.

headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% in September, cementing expectations of a Bank Rate rise

terms.meaning: Consumer Prices Index, the main measure of how fast prices rise.
The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences loan and savings rates.
Inflation leaving out volatile items such as energy and food.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% in September, cementing expectations of a Bank Rate rise
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% economists expected, the Office for National Statistics reported. Motor fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile items, increased to 2.8% from 2.6%, and services inflation went up to 3.7% from 3.4%. Analysts link the energy shock to the US-Iran war and difficulty moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted 6 to 3 in September to hold Bank Rate at 3.75%, with three members wanting a rise to 4%. LSEG data cited by CNBC show markets pricing a 98% chance of a 25 basis point rise next month. October inflation data are due on 18 November.
levels.why: Higher inflation and a likely rate rise raise costs for borrowers and households.

levels.headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% as fuel costs surge
levels.body:
Annual CPI inflation climbed to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August, above the 3.4% forecast. Petrol and diesel prices were up 29.8% on a year earlier, according to the ONS.
Underlying pressures also grew: core inflation reached 2.8% from 2.6%, and services inflation 3.7% from 3.4%. Economists warn this raises the risk of second-round effects beyond energy. The jump is tied to the US-Iran war and disrupted oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Bank of England held Bank Rate at 3.75% in September by six votes to three. Markets now see a 98% chance of a rise to 4% next month, per LSEG data cited by CNBC, with another increase priced for December.
levels.why: It points to dearer borrowing and continued pressure on household budgets.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5%, making an interest rate rise very likely
levels.body:
UK inflation rose to 3.5% in the year to September, from 3.1% in August. Economists had expected 3.4%. The biggest driver was fuel, with motor fuel prices 29.8% higher than a year before.
Core inflation, which strips out energy and food, rose to 2.8%, and services inflation to 3.7%. Economists say this suggests price rises are spreading beyond energy. The oil price jump is linked to the US-Iran war and trouble shipping oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Bank of England kept its main rate at 3.75% in September, with three of nine members wanting a rise. Markets now think a rise to 4% next month is almost certain.
levels.why: Interest rates and prices shape the cost of mortgages and the weekly shop.

levels.headline: Inflation rises to 3.5% and a Bank of England rate rise looks likely
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier, according to official figures. That is up from 3.1% in August and a little more than the 3.4% experts had predicted.
Petrol and diesel were the main cause, costing 29.8% more than a year ago. The price of oil has jumped because of the war between the US and Iran and problems moving oil through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, also rose to 2.8%.
The Bank of England set its main interest rate at 3.75% in September. Traders now think it will go up to 4% next month.
levels.why: Higher rates and prices can make loans dearer and shopping bills bigger.

levels.headline: Prices rise faster as fuel costs jump, and interest rates look set to go up
levels.body:
Prices in the UK rose 3.5% in the year to September. In August the rise was 3.1%. Experts had guessed 3.4%. This measure is called inflation. It shows how much more things cost than a year ago.
Fuel is the main reason. Petrol and diesel cost nearly 30% more than a year earlier. Oil has become dearer because of the war involving the US and Iran. Even if you leave out food and energy, prices are rising a bit faster, at 2.8%.
The Bank of England sets an interest rate that affects loans. It is at 3.75% now. Traders expect it to rise to 4% next month.
levels.why: It affects how much families pay for fuel, loans and food.

levels.headline: Prices are climbing faster, mostly because of fuel
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier. In August the figure was 3.1%. This yearly rise in prices is called inflation, and it was a little higher than the 3.4% experts had expected.
Fuel is the biggest cause. Petrol and diesel cost nearly 30% more than a year ago, because a war involving the US and Iran has made oil harder to move around the world. Prices of services, such as haircuts and train tickets, also rose faster, by 3.7%.
The Bank of England sets the main interest rate, which affects the cost of loans. It is 3.75% now. Most traders expect the Bank to raise it to 4% next month to help slow price rises.
levels.why: It affects what families pay for fuel, shopping and loans.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, and borrowing may get dearer
levels.body:
Inflation is how fast prices go up. In September, prices in the UK were 3.5% higher than a year before. In August it was 3.1%, so things are getting dearer faster.
Petrol and diesel are the main reason. They cost nearly 30% more than a year ago. This is because of a war that involves the US and Iran, which has made oil harder to move around the world. Other prices are creeping up too.
The Bank of England has a main interest rate, now 3.75%. When it goes up, loans such as mortgages usually cost more. Most experts expect it to rise to 4% next month.
levels.why: It affects the cost of fuel, shopping and loans for families.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster, and loans may cost more
levels.body:
Inflation means prices going up over time. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than a year earlier. Last month it was 3.1%. So things are getting dearer a bit faster than before.
The main reason is petrol and diesel, which cost almost 30% more than a year ago. Oil is dearer because of a war involving the US and Iran. Oil ships find it harder to travel, so there is less to go around.
The Bank of England sets an interest rate, now 3.75%. When the rate goes up, borrowing costs more. Many experts think the Bank will raise it to 4% next month.
levels.why: It means families may pay more for fuel and loans.

levels.headline: Why things cost more now, and what may happen next
levels.body:
Inflation is when prices go up. Last month, things cost 3.5% more than a year before. That means a toy that cost 100 pounds last year now costs about 103 pounds and 50 pence.
Petrol is the biggest reason. It costs nearly one third more than last year. There is a war far away that has made it harder to move oil around the world, so oil costs more.
The Bank of England is like a referee for money. It sets an interest rate. If prices rise too fast, it can put the rate up, so borrowing costs more and people spend less. Most experts think it will do that next month.
levels.why: It affects what families pay for petrol, shopping and loans.

levels.headline: Things cost a bit more than before
levels.body:
When shops charge more for things over time, grown-ups call it inflation. Last month, prices were a bit higher than they were last year. If a sweet cost 100 pence a year ago, it might now cost about 103 or 104 pence.
Petrol, which makes cars go, has cost a lot more. A war far away has made oil harder to move around. Oil is used to make petrol, so it costs more.
There is a bank for the whole country called the Bank of England. It can change the price of borrowing money. Grown-ups think it will make borrowing cost a bit more soon, to slow price rises.
levels.why: It helps explain why the family shop and petrol can cost more.

headline: Government blames Iran for RAF Fairford security scare, charges two Iranian nationals

terms.meaning: Penalties, such as freezing assets, imposed on people or countries.
Officially naming who is responsible for an attack or plot.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a powerful armed force.

levels.headline: Government blames Iran for RAF Fairford security scare, charges two Iranian nationals
levels.body:
The UK government has attributed the 27 September security scare at RAF Fairford, a base used by the US, to Iran. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Tehran denies involvement.
Five British men were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences, but police found no explosives, only a quantity of petrol, and the five were released on bail. A Home Secretary statement says two men, both Iranian nationals, have now been charged with terrorism offences, and the UK is sanctioning two individuals accused of espionage and attacks on behalf of Iran.
Foreign ministers from several countries and the EU High Representative backed the attribution. The US later moved its B-1 bombers from the base.
levels.why: It shows how a distant conflict is reaching UK security and foreign policy.

levels.headline: Burnham pins RAF Fairford incident on Iran as charges and sanctions follow
levels.body:
The government has formally attributed the 27 September incident at RAF Fairford to Iran. Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran and almost certainly directed by the Revolutionary Guard. Iran denies this.
Five men arrested after the alarm were released on bail, as police found petrol but no explosives. The Home Secretary has since said two Iranian nationals are charged with terrorism offences, and two individuals are being sanctioned for espionage and attacks carried out for the Iranian state.
A group of foreign ministers and the EU's High Representative endorsed the UK's attribution. President Trump said the US had moved its B-1 bombers from the base after threats he linked to Iran.
levels.why: It tests UK relations with Iran and with allies.

levels.headline: UK blames Iran for the RAF Fairford scare; two Iranian nationals charged
levels.body:
The UK government says Iran was behind the security scare at RAF Fairford on 27 September. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said it was highly likely to have been organised in Iran and directed by its Revolutionary Guard. Iran says this is wrong.
Five British men were first arrested, but police found only petrol and no explosives, and they were freed on bail. Two Iranian nationals have now been charged with terrorism offences. The government has also announced sanctions on two people it says carried out spying and attacks for Iran.
Many other countries backed the UK's claim. The US has since moved its B-1 bombers away from the base.
levels.why: It affects national security and the UK's role in the Middle East crisis.

levels.headline: Government says Iran was behind a security scare at an RAF base
levels.body:
The government says Iran was behind a security scare at RAF Fairford, an airbase used by the US, on 27 September. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was very likely planned in Iran and run by the Revolutionary Guard, a powerful Iranian armed force. Iran denies this.
Five men were arrested at first on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences. Police found petrol but no explosives, and the men were released on bail. Now two Iranian nationals have been charged with terrorism offences. The government is also placing sanctions, which are penalties, on two people it accuses of spying for Iran.
The US has moved its B-1 bombers away from the base.
levels.why: It shows how global conflicts can affect safety and politics at home.

levels.headline: UK says Iran was behind an RAF base scare and charges two men
levels.body:
The UK government says Iran was behind a scare at RAF Fairford on 27 September. This is a base that the US uses. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said Iran very likely planned it, with the Revolutionary Guard in charge. Iran says it is not true.
Five men were arrested first. Police found petrol but no bombs, so the men were let out on bail. Now two Iranian men have been charged with terrorism crimes. The UK has also put sanctions on two people it says spied and carried out attacks for Iran. Sanctions are penalties, such as freezing their money.
Other countries support the UK's view. The US moved its bomber planes away.
levels.why: It affects the safety of the UK and its relations with other countries.

levels.headline: The government says Iran was behind a scare at a military base
levels.body:
On 27 September there was a security scare at RAF Fairford, an airbase in England that the US uses. The government now says Iran was behind it. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was very likely planned in Iran. Iran denies this.
Police first arrested five British men. They found petrol but no explosives, and the men were released on bail. Later, two Iranian nationals were charged with terrorism offences. The government has also put sanctions on two people it accuses of spying and carrying out attacks for Iran. Sanctions are penalties, such as freezing someone's money.
Countries including allies in Europe agreed with the UK's view. The US has moved its large B-1 bomber planes away from the base.
levels.why: It shows how a war far away can touch safety in the UK.

levels.headline: The UK says Iran caused a scare at a military airbase
levels.body:
On 27 September there was a scare at RAF Fairford, an airbase in England that the US uses. The government now says Iran was behind it. Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said it was very likely planned in Iran. Iran says that is not true.
Police first arrested five men. They found petrol but no bombs, so the men were let out on bail. Later, two Iranian men were charged with terrorism crimes. The UK has also punished two people it accuses of spying, by using sanctions. That means freezing their money and limiting what they can do.
The US moved its large bomber planes away from the base.
levels.why: It shows how a war far away can affect safety in the UK.

levels.headline: The UK blames Iran for a scare at an airbase
levels.body:
There is a base called RAF Fairford where planes from the US can stay. On 27 September, there was a scare there. The government says Iran was behind it. The Prime Minister is Andy Burnham. He said Iran very likely planned it. Iran says it did not.
The police arrested five men at first. They found petrol, but no bombs. The men were let out. Later two men from Iran were charged with crimes linked to terrorism. The UK has also punished two people for spying, called sanctions. Many other countries say they agree with the UK.
The US also moved its big bomber planes away from the base.
levels.why: It helps keep the country safe and shows who is working with whom.

levels.headline: Police and the government deal with a scare at a base
levels.body:
A base is a place where planes and soldiers stay. One is called RAF Fairford. On 27 September, something scary happened near it. Police arrested five men but found only petrol, not bombs, so the men were let go for now.
The government is led by the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham. He says Iran, a country far away, very likely planned it. Iran says it did not. Two men from Iran have been charged with crimes. The UK has also stopped two people from using their money, as a punishment.
Planes from the US that stayed at the base have moved away.
levels.why: It is about keeping people safe.

levels.headline: A scare at an airbase, and who the government blames
levels.body:
Imagine a school with a big gate. One day, a scary thing happens near the gate. Police come and take away five people, but they only find a can of petrol. The people are let go for now.
The leader of the country is the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham. He says another country, called Iran, planned the scare. Iran says it did not. Two men from Iran have now been told they are in trouble with the law. The government also stopped two people from using their money.
The big planes from America that stayed at the base have moved to somewhere else.
levels.why: It is about keeping people safe and finding out who did what.

The regulator for oil and gas licences in UK waters.

levels.headline: Jackdaw gas field approved after court ruling, as Burnham and Trump discuss it
levels.body:
The Energy Secretary has agreed that the regulator can grant consent for gas production at the Jackdaw field, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen. The North Sea Transition Authority then issued the consent, and supply could begin from the end of this month. The operator, Adura, is a joint venture between Shell and Equinor.

levels.headline: Energy Secretary approves Jackdaw gas field after the courts demanded a rethink

The Energy Secretary has agreed to consent for gas production at Jackdaw, 150 miles east of Aberdeen, and the North Sea Transition Authority has issued it. Supply could start by the end of the month. Adura, a Shell and Equinor venture, operates the field.

levels.headline: Jackdaw gas field gets green light, with supply due from the end of October

The Energy Secretary has approved gas production at the Jackdaw field, around 150 miles east of Aberdeen, and the regulator, the North Sea Transition Authority, has granted consent. Gas could flow from the end of this month. The field is run by Adura, a joint venture of Shell and Equinor.

levels.headline: UK approves Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea

The government has approved the Jackdaw gas field, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen. The regulator has issued consent and gas could start flowing at the end of October. A company called Adura, owned by Shell and Equinor, will run it.

levels.why: It shows the tension between energy supply and climate targets.

levels.headline: Government gives the go-ahead to a North Sea gas field
levels.body:
The government has said yes to a gas field called Jackdaw, in the North Sea about 150 miles from Aberdeen. The regulator has given permission, and gas could start to flow at the end of October. Shell and Equinor run the project through a firm called Adura.
Ministers say it could add about 6% to the gas the UK produces at its busiest, for up to 11 years. They say this fits their promise not to give out new licences to look for oil and gas. The Prime Minister spoke to President Trump about it.
levels.why: It affects energy supplies, jobs and efforts to tackle climate change.

levels.headline: Government says yes to a North Sea gas field, and some people are unhappy
levels.body:
The government has approved a gas field called Jackdaw in the North Sea, about 150 miles from Aberdeen. The regulator has given permission, and gas could start to flow at the end of October. The firms Shell and Equinor run it together.
Ministers say it could add about 6% to the gas the UK produces at its busiest, for up to 11 years. Gas is used to heat homes and make electricity. Some people argue that burning gas makes climate change worse. A Scottish court said in January 2025 that the first approval was unlawful because it ignored this harm, so the decision was made again.
The Prime Minister talked about it with President Trump on 23 October.
levels.why: It balances energy supplies and jobs against the fight against climate change.

levels.headline: The government says yes to a North Sea gas field
levels.body:
The government has agreed that a gas field called Jackdaw can start work. It is in the North Sea, about 150 miles from Aberdeen. The gas could start flowing at the end of October. Two firms, Shell and Equinor, run it together.
Ministers say it could add about 6% to the gas the UK makes, for up to 11 years. Gas heats homes and makes electricity. Some people worry that burning gas harms the climate. A court in Scotland said the first yes was wrong because nobody had checked that harm. So the government had to decide again, and it said yes.
The Prime Minister talked about it with US President Trump.
levels.why: It affects energy and the fight against climate change.

levels.headline: A new gas field is allowed to start
levels.body:
The government has said a gas field called Jackdaw can start. It is under the sea, a long way off the coast of Scotland. Gas from it could begin to flow at the end of October. It is run by two big companies, Shell and Equinor.
Gas is used to heat homes and make electricity. The government says this field will give the UK about 6% more gas than it makes now, for up to 11 years. Some people worry that burning gas is bad for the planet. A court said the government had to think about that harm first, so it decided again.
The leader of the UK talked about it with the US president.
levels.why: It is about heating our homes and looking after the planet.

levels.headline: A new gas field gets the green light
levels.body:
Gas is something we burn to cook food and to heat our homes. Some gas lies deep under the sea. A company wants to dig for it at a place called Jackdaw, far from the coast of Scotland. The government has said it can begin.
The company hopes gas will start to flow at the end of October. The government says it will give the UK a little more gas of its own, for about eleven years. But burning gas makes the air warmer, which is bad for the planet. A court asked the government to think about that again, and it still said yes.
Some people agree and some do not.
levels.why: It is about heating homes and also caring for the planet.

levels.headline: Digging for gas under the sea: should we?
levels.body:
Some of the gas that warms our homes comes from deep under the sea. A place called Jackdaw has some. The grown-ups in charge of the country have said that companies can now dig it up. They hope it will start at the end of the month.
The government says this will give us a little more of our own gas to use. Some people are cross, because burning gas makes the Earth warmer. A court once said the leaders must think about that carefully, and they did, and still said yes.
It is a bit like deciding whether to eat a sweet now, even though it is not so good for your teeth. People disagree about it.
levels.why: It is about keeping homes warm while looking after the Earth.

headline: UK retail sales fall 0.4% in September while unemployment stands at 4.7%

terms.meaning: The total value of goods bought in shops and online.
The share of people looking for work who cannot find a job.
The Office for National Statistics, the UK's official statistics agency.

levels.headline: UK retail sales fall 0.4% in September while unemployment stands at 4.7%
levels.body:
UK retail sales fell 0.4% in September compared with August, a bigger drop than economists expected, according to Trading Economics figures from the ONS release of 23 October. They were 0.8% higher than a year earlier. Sales excluding fuel fell 0.7% on the month.
The ONS said retail sales still rose in the third quarter as a whole, by its first estimate. Its monthly GDP release of 15 October noted that consumer demand indicators weakened in September and that retail footfall fell.
In the labour market, the ONS reported on 20 October that unemployment was 4.7%, down 0.1 percentage points on both the year and the quarter. Employment reached 34.577 million, an employment rate of 75.3%. The next GDP figures are due on 12 November.
levels.why: Shop sales and jobs show how households are coping with higher prices.

levels.headline: Retail sales drop 0.4% in September; jobless rate at 4.7%
levels.body:
Retail sales volumes in Great Britain fell 0.4% in September from August, worse than forecasts of 0.1%. Year on year they rose 0.8%. Sales excluding fuel dropped 0.7% in the month, based on Trading Economics figures from the ONS release of 23 October.
The ONS still estimates that sales grew over the third quarter. Its 15 October GDP release said consumer demand weakened in September, with lower footfall.
The labour market looks steadier. Unemployment was 4.7%, down 0.1 points on the quarter and the year, and employment reached 34.577 million, or 75.3% of working-age people. GDP figures arrive on 12 November.
levels.why: The figures show whether shoppers are cutting back as prices rise.

levels.headline: Shoppers cut back in September as jobs market stays steady
levels.body:
UK retail sales fell 0.4% in September, more than the 0.1% fall economists had expected. They were still 0.8% up on a year earlier. Without fuel, sales dropped 0.7%. The figures come from the ONS release on 23 October.
Over the whole of July to September, sales rose slightly, according to the ONS. But official data on the economy said shopper demand weakened in September and fewer people visited shops.
The jobs picture is steadier. Unemployment was 4.7%, which is 0.1 percentage points lower than a year earlier and than the previous quarter. There were 34.577 million people in work. Official GDP figures are next due on 12 November.
levels.why: It tells us how the economy is doing as prices rise.

levels.headline: Shop sales fall in September, but fewer people are out of work
levels.body:
UK shop sales fell 0.4% in September compared with August. Experts had expected a smaller fall of 0.1%. Compared with a year ago, sales were still up 0.8%. If you leave out fuel, sales fell by 0.7%.
The Office for National Statistics says sales rose across July, August and September taken together. Its other figures said people were spending a bit less in September and fewer were visiting shops.
There was better news on jobs. About 4.7% of people looking for work were unemployed, slightly less than a year ago. In total, 34.577 million people were in work. The next economic growth figures come out on 12 November.
levels.why: Spending and jobs show how well households are coping.

levels.headline: People spent less in the shops in September
levels.body:
The UK's shops sold less in September than in August. The drop was 0.4%, which was bigger than experts thought. Compared with a year ago, shops still sold 0.8% more. Without petrol and diesel, sales fell by 0.7%.
The Office for National Statistics counts these sales. It says that across July, August and September, shops did sell a bit more. But in September, people spent less, and fewer walked into shops.
There was better news about jobs. Around 4.7% of people who wanted a job did not have one. That is a little lower than a year ago. In all, 34.577 million people had jobs.
levels.why: It helps show whether families can afford things as prices rise.

levels.headline: Shoppers spent a little less in September, but unemployment is lower than last year
levels.body:
Shops in the UK sold 0.4% less in September than in August. Experts had expected a smaller fall. Compared with a year ago, shops still sold 0.8% more. If you leave out petrol and diesel, sales fell by 0.7%.
Over July, August and September taken together, sales were a bit higher, according to the Office for National Statistics. But in September people spent less and fewer went into shops.
There was better news about jobs. About 4.7% of people who wanted work were unemployed, a little less than a year ago. In total, 34.577 million people were in work. The next figures on economic growth come out on 12 November.
levels.why: Spending and jobs show how well families are coping with higher prices.

levels.headline: Shops sold less in September, but jobs numbers were steady
levels.body:
Shops in the UK sold a little less in September than in August. The fall was 0.4%. Experts had thought it would be smaller. Compared with a year ago, shops still sold 0.8% more. Without petrol, sales fell more, by 0.7%.
Sales across July, August and September together were a bit higher, official figures say. But in September people spent less, and fewer went into shops.
There was better news about work. About 4.7 in every 100 people who wanted a job did not have one. That is a little better than last year. In all, about 34.6 million people had jobs.
levels.why: It tells us if people are spending and if there are enough jobs.

levels.headline: Shops had fewer sales, but many people still have jobs
levels.body:
In September, shops in the UK sold a little less than in August. The fall was small, 0.4%. That means for every 1,000 pounds of things sold in August, shops sold about 996 pounds in September. Prices are rising, so people may be more careful with money.
The good news is about jobs. About 4.7 in every 100 people who wanted a job could not find one. That is a little lower than a year ago. About 34.6 million people were working.
The people who count these things are called the Office for National Statistics. They will share more news on 12 November.
levels.why: It shows how families are managing as things cost more.

levels.headline: People bought a little less in September
levels.body:
A shop sells things like clothes, toys and food. In September, shops sold a little less than in August. If a shop sold 100 sweets in August, it sold about 99 or 100 in September. That is a small dip, but experts noticed it.
When prices go up, people may buy less, a bit like having less pocket money to spend. But many people still have jobs. About 95 in every 100 people who want to work have a job. That is a bit better than last year.
Grown-ups will look at new numbers again on 12 November.
levels.why: It shows how families are coping when things cost more.

levels.headline: Shops had a quieter month, but lots of people are working
levels.body:
Think of a school tuck shop. In one month it sold a little bit less than the month before. That is what happened to shops across the UK in September. They sold about 4 in every 1,000 pounds less than in August.
When things cost more, people sometimes buy fewer things. Their money does not stretch as far, like when your pocket money has to last longer.
But there was good news. Nearly all grown-ups who wanted a job had one. About 95 out of 100 had work, which was a bit better than last year.
levels.why: It tells us if families are doing OK with their money.

headline: Gulf braces for renewed US-Iran war as Trump signals action after the 3 November midterms

terms.meaning: A narrow sea passage through which a large share of the world's oil ships.
US elections held halfway through a president's term.
An Iran-backed armed group based in Yemen.

levels.headline: Gulf braces for renewed US-Iran war as Trump signals action after the 3 November midterms
levels.body:
President Trump has said US forces would hold off attacking Iran until after the midterm elections on 3 November. The New York Times reported that the US and Israeli militaries have drawn up plans for renewed strikes, aimed at Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone stocks. On 22 October Mr Trump said the US was not negotiating with Iran and that something would happen "fairly soon".
The State Department has ordered non-emergency US government staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis. Riyadh's airport has been hit repeatedly, and a Saudi Aramco administrative building in Dhahran was struck on Tuesday.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard chief said Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can sink American warships. Gulf states are bracing for a possible return to all-out war.
levels.why: The conflict is already pushing up oil and fuel prices worldwide.

levels.headline: US reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms as Houthis hit Saudi sites
levels.body:
Mr Trump has said the US will wait until after the 3 November midterms before attacking Iran. According to the New York Times, US and Israeli planners have prepared strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and arsenals of missiles and drones. On 22 October Mr Trump said no negotiations were taking place and that something would happen "fairly soon".
Washington has ordered non-emergency staff out of Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks. Riyadh's airport has been struck several times, and Aramco's Dhahran headquarters took a hit on Tuesday.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard chief said Tehran was "counting the moments" until it could sink US warships, and Gulf governments are preparing for a return to full-scale war.
levels.why: It could disrupt oil supplies and raise prices for people everywhere.

levels.headline: US says it will wait until after the midterms before striking Iran
levels.body:
President Trump has said the US will not attack Iran until after the midterm elections on 3 November. The New York Times reports that the US and Israel have drawn up plans for new strikes on Iran's energy sites, nuclear sites and missile and drone stores. On 22 October Mr Trump said the US was not negotiating and that something would happen "fairly soon".
The US has ordered non-emergency staff to leave Saudi Arabia because the Houthis, an Iran-backed group, have attacked it. Riyadh airport has been hit several times and a Saudi Aramco office building was struck on Tuesday.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it is "counting the moments" until it can strike US warships.
levels.why: It matters for safety in the region and for global oil prices.

levels.headline: Trump holds off Iran strikes until after the US elections, but tension is rising
levels.body:
President Trump says the US will wait until after its midterm elections on 3 November before attacking Iran. Reports say the US and Israel have drawn up plans to hit Iran's energy sites, nuclear sites and missile stores. On 22 October Mr Trump said the US was not talking to Iran and that something would happen "fairly soon".
Meanwhile the Houthis, an armed group backed by Iran, have attacked Saudi Arabia. Riyadh airport has been hit many times and an office building of the oil company Aramco was struck. The US has told non-emergency staff to leave Saudi Arabia.
Iran's military leaders say they are waiting for a chance to strike US ships.
levels.why: It could affect oil prices and the safety of millions of people.

levels.headline: US waits until after elections to hit Iran, but fear of war is growing
levels.body:
President Trump says the US will wait until after its midterm elections on 3 November before attacking Iran. These are elections held halfway through a president's time in office. Reports say the US and Israel have drawn up plans to hit Iranian oil sites, nuclear sites and weapons stores. Mr Trump says the US is not talking to Iran and that something will happen "fairly soon".
An armed group called the Houthis, backed by Iran, has attacked Saudi Arabia, including an airport and an oil company building. The US has told some staff to leave the country.
Countries in the Gulf are getting ready for a bigger war.
levels.why: A war in this region can push up oil prices and affect fuel costs worldwide.

levels.headline: The US says it will wait until after its elections before it hits Iran
levels.body:
President Trump says the US will wait until after its midterm elections on 3 November before attacking Iran. Midterms are elections held halfway through a president's time in office. Reports say the US and Israel have drawn up plans to hit Iran's energy sites, nuclear sites and weapons stores. Mr Trump says the US is not negotiating and that something will happen "fairly soon".
The Houthis, an armed group backed by Iran, have attacked Saudi Arabia, including an airport in Riyadh and an office of the oil company Aramco. The US has told non-emergency staff to leave Saudi Arabia.
Countries around the Gulf are getting ready for a bigger war.
levels.why: It could change oil prices and put many people in danger.

levels.headline: The US may attack Iran after its elections, and neighbours are worried
levels.body:
The US president, Donald Trump, says the US will wait until after its elections on 3 November before attacking Iran. Reports say the US and Israel have made plans to hit Iran's oil sites, nuclear sites and weapons. Mr Trump says the US is not talking with Iran and that something will happen "fairly soon".
A group called the Houthis, who are friends of Iran, have been attacking Saudi Arabia. They hit an airport in the capital, Riyadh, and an office of a big oil company. The US has told some of its workers to leave Saudi Arabia.
Countries near Iran are getting ready in case a big war starts again.
levels.why: It could make oil and petrol more expensive and put many people in danger.

levels.headline: The US and Iran: a war that may start again
levels.body:
The US and Iran have been in a war. The US president, Donald Trump, says the US will not attack Iran again until after its elections on 3 November. But some news reports say the US and Israel already have plans ready. Mr Trump says the two sides are not talking and that something will happen soon.
A group called the Houthis helps Iran. They have been attacking Saudi Arabia, a country nearby. They hit an airport and a building owned by an oil company. The US has told some of its workers to leave Saudi Arabia to keep them safe.
People in the area are getting ready for more fighting.
levels.why: It could change the price of oil and put many people in danger.

levels.headline: A war between two countries may start up again
levels.body:
The United States and Iran are two countries that have been fighting. The US leader, Donald Trump, says the US will wait until after its big vote on 3 November before it attacks again. News reports say the US and a friend, Israel, have made plans.
Mr Trump says the two countries are not talking. A group that helps Iran has attacked a nearby country, Saudi Arabia. They hit an airport. The US has told some of its workers to leave Saudi Arabia to stay safe.
People nearby are scared. They are getting ready in case the fighting begins again.
levels.why: It could put many people in danger and make petrol cost more.

levels.headline: Two countries that are fighting may fight again
levels.body:
Imagine two groups in a playground who had a big argument. For now they have stopped, but they are still cross. One leader, from the US, says he will wait until after an important vote on 3 November. Then he may start the argument again.
A friend of Iran has been bothering a nearby country, Saudi Arabia. They hit an airport. The US told some of its workers to leave Saudi Arabia so they stay safe.
People who live nearby are scared and getting ready. Grown-ups all over the world are watching, because fighting there can make petrol cost more.
levels.why: It affects the safety of many people and the cost of petrol.

headline: Brent crude settles at $116.72, its highest since April, as Middle East tensions mount

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil.
West Texas Intermediate, the main US oil benchmark.
The final price of a trading session.

levels.headline: Brent crude settles at $116.72, its highest since April, as Middle East tensions mount
levels.body:
Brent crude futures rose 3.1% on Friday 23 October to settle at $116.72 a barrel, the highest settlement for the international benchmark since 29 April. US West Texas Intermediate gained 3.8% to settle at $103.27 a barrel.
Brent rose 6.2% over the week, its third weekly gain in a row. It had closed at $109.55 on Monday, $108.79 on Tuesday and $108.82 on Wednesday, before jumping 4% to $113.17 on Thursday.
CNBC links the rise to Middle East risk: attacks on tankers, Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia, and fears of renewed US action against Iran after the 3 November midterms. Higher oil costs feed into petrol prices and inflation worldwide.
levels.why: Oil prices feed straight into petrol, transport and food costs.

levels.headline: Brent hits six-month high at $116.72 as Gulf risks grow
levels.body:
Brent futures settled at $116.72 a barrel on Friday 23 October, up 3.1% and the highest close since 29 April. US benchmark WTI rose 3.8% to $103.27.
Over the week Brent gained 6.2%, a third straight weekly rise. Monday's close was $109.55, then $108.79 on Tuesday and $108.82 on Wednesday, before Thursday's 4% jump to $113.17.
The driver is supply fear. Tankers have been attacked, the Houthis have struck Saudi Arabia, and investors expect the US to resume strikes on Iran after the midterms. CNBC notes some reports differ on the timing of any strikes.
levels.why: It raises fuel costs and adds to inflation.

levels.headline: Oil prices climb to a six-month high
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose 3.1% on Friday 23 October to $116.72 a barrel. That is the highest closing price since 29 April. The main US benchmark, WTI, rose 3.8% to $103.27 a barrel.
Brent gained 6.2% across the week, its third weekly rise in a row. It was $109.55 on Monday and $113.17 on Thursday.
The main reason is fear of disruption in the Middle East. Oil tankers have been attacked, a group called the Houthis has struck Saudi Arabia, and investors think the US may attack Iran again after its elections on 3 November.
levels.why: Higher oil prices raise petrol bills and push up inflation.

levels.headline: Oil jumps to its highest since April on fears of a wider Middle East war
levels.body:
The price of oil rose again on Friday 23 October. Brent crude, the benchmark used around the world, closed at $116.72 a barrel, up 3.1%. That is its highest closing price since April. The US benchmark, called WTI, closed at $103.27.
Oil has now risen for three weeks in a row. Over this week alone, Brent went up 6.2%.
The reason is worry about supply. Oil tankers have been attacked and a group called the Houthis has hit targets in Saudi Arabia, a huge oil producer. Investors also think the US may attack Iran again after its elections on 3 November.
levels.why: It makes petrol, heating and shipping more expensive.

levels.headline: Oil costs more than it has for six months
levels.body:
Oil became more expensive again on Friday 23 October. A barrel of Brent crude, which sets the price around the world, cost $116.72 at the end of the day. That is 3.1% more than the day before, and the highest since April. A barrel of US oil cost $103.27.
Oil has become dearer for three weeks in a row. This week alone the price rose 6.2%.
The reason is worry that less oil will reach buyers. Ships carrying oil have been attacked, and a group called the Houthis has struck Saudi Arabia, which makes a lot of oil. People also fear the US may attack Iran again after its elections.
levels.why: Dearer oil means dearer petrol and higher prices in shops.

levels.headline: Oil reaches its highest price since April
levels.body:
The price of oil rose again on Friday 23 October. A barrel of Brent crude, the benchmark used around the world, cost $116.72 at the close, up 3.1% on the day. That is the highest since 29 April. A barrel of the main US kind, WTI, cost $103.27.
Oil has risen for three weeks in a row. This week alone Brent went up 6.2%.
The main reason is worry about supply. Oil tankers have been attacked, and a group called the Houthis has struck Saudi Arabia, which produces a lot of oil. Investors also think the US may attack Iran again after its elections on 3 November. When oil costs more, petrol and transport costs usually follow.
levels.why: Dearer oil raises petrol bills and can push up prices in the shops.

levels.headline: Oil is getting more expensive again
levels.body:
Oil is the thick liquid from the ground that is used to make petrol. A barrel of the main kind, called Brent, cost $116.72 on Friday 23 October. That is the most it has cost since April. It has been going up for three weeks in a row.
Why? People are worried that less oil will reach the shops and petrol stations. Ships carrying oil have been attacked. A group called the Houthis has attacked Saudi Arabia, which sells lots of oil. People also worry that the US and Iran may fight again.
When oil costs more, petrol costs more, and so do many things that are moved in lorries.
levels.why: It makes petrol and many other things cost more.

levels.headline: The price of oil keeps rising
levels.body:
Oil comes from deep in the ground. We use it to make petrol for cars and lorries. On Friday 23 October a barrel of oil cost about 117 dollars. That is the highest price for six months. It has gone up three weeks in a row.
People worry there may be less oil to buy. Some ships carrying oil have been attacked. A group has hit Saudi Arabia, a country that sells a huge amount of oil. People also fear that the US and Iran may start fighting again.
When oil costs more, petrol costs more. Food and other things can cost more too, because lorries use petrol.
levels.why: It means petrol and shopping can cost families more.

levels.headline: Oil is costing more and more
levels.body:
Oil is a liquid from deep underground. Petrol is made from it. This week, oil got more expensive for the third week in a row. A barrel cost about 117 dollars on Friday. It has not cost that much for six months.
Some people are fighting in the Middle East, where lots of oil comes from. Ships carrying oil have been attacked, and so have places in Saudi Arabia. When there may be less oil, sellers ask for more money.
When oil costs more, petrol costs more too. Lorries use petrol to bring food to shops, so food can cost more.
levels.why: It can make petrol and food cost more for families.

levels.headline: Why petrol may cost more soon
levels.body:
Imagine your school sells lemonade at a fair, and the lemons come from a faraway farm. If someone blocks the road to the farm, the lemons get harder to get. Then the farm asks for more money for each lemon.
Oil is a bit like that. It comes from places in the Middle East where there is fighting. Ships have been attacked, and so have places in Saudi Arabia. So oil cost about 117 dollars a barrel on Friday. That is the most for six months.
Cars use petrol, which is made from oil, so petrol may cost more too.
levels.why: It can make petrol and shopping cost more for families.

headline: Cost-of-living protests continue in France as unrest spreads across Europe

terms.meaning: What people have to pay for everyday things such as food, fuel and rent.
People who gather to protest in public.
Regular money paid to people after they retire.

levels.headline: Cost-of-living protests continue in France as unrest spreads across Europe
levels.body:
A new round of protests took place across France on Saturday 24 October. Organisers said more than 800,000 people joined demonstrations nationwide, including 250,000 in Paris, while authorities put the national figure at 410,000. Police fired tear gas at a smaller protest in Lyon.
The movement began with high school students angry about school conditions and widened into a broader protest about living costs, fuel prices and public services. Demonstrations on 17 October turned violent, with looting, fires at town halls and more than 2,000 arrests reported.
Euronews also reported clashes in several Italian cities, with soldiers patrolling Milan, water cannon and tear gas used against demonstrators in Tirana, Albania, and pensioners marching in Madrid for better pensions.
levels.why: It shows how higher prices are fuelling political anger across Europe.

levels.headline: Hundreds of thousands march in France as cost-of-living anger spreads
levels.body:
Protests continued across France on Saturday 24 October. Organisers claimed more than 800,000 marchers nationwide, with 250,000 in Paris; authorities counted 410,000. Police used tear gas on a smaller protest in Lyon.
It started with high school students complaining about school conditions, then grew into a wider protest over living costs, fuel prices and public services. The 17 October demonstrations turned violent, with looting, fires at town halls and more than 2,000 arrests reported.
Euronews reported unrest elsewhere too: clashes in Italian cities with soldiers patrolling Milan, water cannon and tear gas in Tirana, and a pensioners' march in Madrid.
levels.why: Prices and public services are driving political tension in several countries.

levels.headline: Protests in France draw hundreds of thousands, and unrest spreads across Europe
levels.body:
On Saturday 24 October, big protests took place across France. Organisers said over 800,000 people took part, including 250,000 in Paris. The authorities said 410,000. Police fired tear gas at a smaller protest in Lyon.
The protests began with school students upset about conditions in their schools. They have grown into a wider movement about the cost of living, fuel prices and public services. On 17 October the protests turned violent, with looting, fires at town halls and more than 2,000 arrests.
There was also trouble elsewhere. Clashes broke out in several Italian cities, police used water cannon in Albania, and pensioners marched in Madrid.
levels.why: It shows how the cost of living is fuelling anger in several countries.

levels.headline: Big protests in France as anger over prices spreads across Europe

levels.why: Rising prices are causing anger and unrest in many places.

levels.headline: Hundreds of thousands protest in France about high prices

levels.why: It shows that high prices are making many people angry.

levels.headline: Big crowds march in France because things cost too much

levels.headline: People in France are protesting about prices

On Saturday, a very large number of people marched in France. Some say it was 800,000 people and the police say it was 410,000. Either way, it was a lot. In one city, police used tear gas on some marchers.
It began with school students who were not happy about their schools. Then lots more people joined. They are cross because things cost too much, like food and petrol. They also want better schools and hospitals. A week before, some marches got violent, and over 2,000 people were arrested.

levels.why: It shows that high prices are upsetting lots of people.

levels.headline: Lots of people march in France
levels.body:
In France, lots of people walked through the streets together on Saturday. This is called a protest. They wanted to show they are unhappy. Some say 800,000 people came. The police say 410,000. That is still enough to fill many football stadiums.
It began with school students who did not like the state of their schools. Then more people joined. They are cross that food and petrol cost so much. Some marches a week earlier turned rough, and many people were arrested.

levels.why: It shows that when prices go up, many people feel worried and cross.

levels.headline: Why people are marching in France
levels.body:
Imagine the tuck shop doubles its prices and nobody has more pocket money. Lots of children would feel cross. Something like that is happening to grown-ups in France. Food, petrol and other things cost a lot, so many people feel worried.
On Saturday, lots of them walked through the streets together. This is called a protest. Some say 800,000 people came and some say 410,000. It began with school students who wanted better schools, then many other people joined.

headline: Moody's keeps France at Aa3 with negative outlook as bond yields hit 5%

terms.meaning: A grade showing how likely a borrower is to repay its debts.
The return investors demand for lending to a government; it rises when lenders feel more risk.
The gap when a government spends more than it collects in taxes.

levels.headline: Moody's keeps France at Aa3 with negative outlook as bond yields hit 5%
levels.body:
Moody's kept France's credit rating at Aa3, a level it still calls high grade, but left its outlook negative, citing the risk that political fragmentation keeps hampering parliament's work. CNBC describes the decision as a brief reprieve rather than a vote of confidence. S&P and Fitch had already downgraded France in 2025.
The 10-year French bond yield briefly topped 5% on Wednesday 21 October, the first time since 2002, after the unrest of recent weeks. The deficit is projected at about 5.4% of GDP this year and public debt at roughly 119% of GDP.
Analysts see the ECB as unlikely to step in soon. Oxford Economics warns that a severe bond-market shock could push France and Italy into recession in 2027, though it is not its central forecast.
levels.why: France's borrowing costs affect the eurozone and the wider European economy.

levels.headline: France keeps Aa3 rating with a negative outlook as borrowing costs reach 5%
levels.body:
Moody's left France's rating at Aa3 but kept a negative outlook, warning that political fragmentation could keep hampering parliament. CNBC calls it a reprieve, not a show of confidence. S&P and Fitch cut France in 2025.
The 10-year yield briefly passed 5% on Wednesday 21 October for the first time since 2002 as protests unsettled markets. The deficit is forecast at about 5.4% of GDP this year, and debt at about 119% of GDP.
A Goldman Sachs strategist said conditions did not warrant emergency ECB action. Oxford Economics says a severe bond shock could tip France and Italy into recession in 2027, though that is outside its central forecast.
levels.why: High French yields can spill over to other eurozone countries.

levels.headline: Credit rating agency Moody's holds France's rating, but warns about politics
levels.body:
Moody's kept France's credit rating at Aa3, which it still calls high grade. But it left its outlook negative, because political divisions could keep stopping parliament from getting things done. CNBC says it is a short reprieve. Two other agencies, S&P and Fitch, downgraded France in 2025.
France's cost of borrowing has jumped. The 10-year bond yield briefly passed 5% on Wednesday 21 October, the first time since 2002, after weeks of protests. France is expected to run a deficit of about 5.4% of GDP this year, and its debt is about 119% of GDP.
Analysts think the European Central Bank is unlikely to step in soon.
levels.why: It shows how politics and debt can combine to raise borrowing costs.

levels.headline: France's credit rating is held, but its borrowing is getting costly
levels.body:
Moody's, an agency that grades how safe it is to lend to a country, kept France at Aa3, which is still a high grade. But it said the outlook is negative. The reason is that political splits could stop parliament from working well. Two other agencies lowered France's grade in 2025.
France borrows by selling bonds. The return investors ask for on 10-year bonds briefly went above 5% on Wednesday 21 October, the first time since 2002, as protests worried markets. France spends about 5.4% of its national income more than it collects this year, and its debts are about 119% of its income.
The European Central Bank is not expected to step in soon.
levels.why: If France's borrowing costs rise, it can affect other European countries.

levels.headline: France keeps its credit grade, but borrowing costs have jumped
levels.body:
A credit rating is a grade that shows how safe it is to lend money to someone. The agency Moody's kept France at Aa3, which is still a good grade. France borrows by selling bonds. Lenders now want a higher return. On Wednesday the return on 10-year bonds went above 5%, the first time since 2002. This follows weeks of protests. France is also spending more than it collects, and its debts are large.
The European Central Bank is not expected to step in yet.
levels.why: If it costs France more to borrow, it can hurt other European countries too.

levels.headline: France keeps its credit rating, but borrowing is getting dearer

levels.headline: France keeps a good money grade, but things look shaky
levels.body:
A credit rating is like a school grade for how safe it is to lend money to a country. The agency Moody's kept France on a good grade. But it said the future looks shaky. France's politicians are divided and it is hard for them to agree on things.
France borrows money by selling bonds. Lenders now ask for more in return, because they feel nervous. On Wednesday the rate went above 5%. That has not happened since 2002. People have also been protesting in the streets for weeks.
France spends more than it collects in taxes, and it owes a lot.
levels.why: If France has to pay more to borrow, it can affect people across Europe.

levels.headline: France keeps its money grade, but borrowing is costly
levels.body:
A credit rating is a grade for how safe it is to lend money to a country. An agency called Moody's gave France a good grade and kept it. But it said the future looks a bit shaky, because France's politicians are divided and find it hard to agree.
When a country borrows, it pays extra money called interest. France now has to pay more than 5% a year on some loans. That has not happened since 2002. People are also protesting in the streets about prices.
France spends more than it takes in, and it owes a lot of money. Experts are watching closely.
levels.why: If it costs France more to borrow, it can affect other countries too.

levels.headline: Money worries in France
levels.body:
Imagine borrowing money from a friend. If your friend thinks you might not pay it back, they ask you to pay extra. That extra is called interest. Countries borrow money too. France has to pay more than 5 in every 100 for some of its loans. That is a lot.
A company called Moody's gives countries grades, a bit like a school report. It kept France on a good grade. But it said the future looks shaky because France's leaders are not agreeing with each other.
France also spends more than it collects, and it owes lots of money.
levels.why: It shows why countries need to manage their money carefully.

levels.headline: France has a money worry
levels.body:
A country is a bit like a very big family. Sometimes it borrows money. When it does, it has to pay a little extra, called interest. France now has to pay quite a lot extra. That is a worry.
A company called Moody's gives countries a grade, a bit like a school report. It kept France's grade the same. But it wrote that things might get worse, because France's leaders are not agreeing.
France owes lots of money. Grown-ups all over Europe are watching, because what happens to France can matter to other countries too.
levels.why: It matters because countries near each other share money worries.

headline: Ukraine says Starlink connection restored, but dispute with Musk and Washington continues

terms.meaning: A satellite internet service run by SpaceX.
A military-focused version of Starlink.
An agreement to stop fighting, at least for a time.

levels.headline: Ukraine says Starlink connection restored, but dispute with Musk and Washington continues
levels.body:
Ukraine said on Saturday 24 October that its connection to Starlink and the military-focused Starshield service was stable again, with speeds restored on equipment moving faster than 400 km/h. SpaceX chief Elon Musk said the restriction was imposed because Kyiv violated Starlink's terms of service and that a loophole had been closed the previous week.
The picture remains contested. On Friday, President Zelenskyy had said the restrictions were still there and the speed had not been restored. President Trump confirmed he had asked Mr Musk to ease the curbs after earlier saying he had not spoken to him. Silicon Valley Democrats in the House have asked the White House to investigate who ordered the throttling.
Separately, envoy Steve Witkoff met Mr Zelenskyy in Oslo and was due to travel to Moscow to meet President Putin.
levels.why: Ukraine depends on satellite links for military communications.

levels.headline: Kyiv reports stable Starlink link as Musk, Trump and Zelenskyy give conflicting accounts
levels.body:
Ukraine said on 24 October that Starlink and Starshield connectivity was restored, including on equipment moving above 400 km/h. Elon Musk said access had been restricted because Kyiv broke the terms of service, and that the loophole was shut last week.
On Friday Zelenskyy said the limits remained and speed had not been restored. Mr Trump confirmed a Wall Street Journal report that he asked Mr Musk to ease the restrictions, having earlier said he had not spoken to him. House Democrats want a White House investigation into who ordered the slowdown.
Envoy Steve Witkoff met Mr Zelenskyy in Oslo and was due to travel to Moscow for talks with President Putin.
levels.why: It shows how dependent Ukraine's defence is on one private firm.

levels.headline: Ukraine says its Starlink connection is restored, but questions remain
levels.body:
Ukraine said on Saturday 24 October that its Starlink and Starshield satellite connections were stable again, including on equipment moving faster than 400 km/h. Elon Musk, who runs SpaceX, said access had been limited because Ukraine broke the service's rules, and he said the gap had been closed last week.
On Friday, President Zelenskyy had said the limits were still in place. President Trump said he had asked Mr Musk to ease the limits. Some US lawmakers want an investigation into who slowed the service.
A US envoy, Steve Witkoff, met Mr Zelenskyy in Oslo and was due to go to Moscow to meet President Putin.
levels.why: Ukraine's army relies on these links to communicate.

Ukraine said on Saturday 24 October that its Starlink and Starshield satellite internet was working well again, including on fast-moving equipment. Elon Musk, the head of SpaceX, said the speed had been cut because Ukraine broke the rules of the service. He said a loophole was closed last week.

levels.headline: Ukraine says its satellite internet is back

Ukraine said on Saturday 24 October that its satellite internet, called Starlink, was working well again. Its army also uses a military version called Starshield. Elon Musk, who owns the company, said he had slowed it because Ukraine broke the rules. He said a loophole was closed last week.

levels.headline: Ukraine's satellite internet works again after a slowdown

Ukraine's army uses a satellite internet service called Starlink, run by the company SpaceX. Over recent days it ran slowly. On Saturday 24 October, Ukraine said it was working well again.

levels.headline: Ukraine's army gets its satellite internet back

Ukraine is at war with Russia. Its soldiers use the internet from satellites in space. This is called Starlink. It is owned by a company run by a man called Elon Musk. Over the last few days it went slow.

levels.why: Soldiers need good internet to send messages safely.

levels.headline: Ukraine's soldiers get their space internet back
