Ukraine is in a war. Its soldiers use internet that comes from satellites in space, called Starlink. A man called Elon Musk runs the company that owns it. For a few days the internet was slow.
On Saturday, Ukraine said it was fast again. Mr Musk said he had slowed it because Ukraine broke a rule. The leader of the US, Donald Trump, asked him to make it faster.
Soldiers need good internet to talk to each other. Some leaders are also meeting to talk about how to stop the war.
levels.why: Soldiers need good internet to stay safe.

levels.headline: The internet from space is back for soldiers
levels.body:
Imagine your class has a walkie-talkie for talking to each other, and one day it gets slow and crackly. That is what happened to soldiers in Ukraine. Their internet comes from satellites far above the Earth. A man called Elon Musk runs the company.
For some days it was slow. Then on Saturday Ukraine said it worked well again. Mr Musk said he had slowed it because a rule was broken. The leader of the US asked him to make it faster.
Soldiers need to talk to each other to stay safe.
levels.why: Soldiers need good ways to talk to each other to stay safe.

headline: Fed expected to hold rates at 27-28 October meeting, with a December hike priced in

terms.meaning: The central bank of the United States.
An increase in the main interest rate.
Hints from a central bank about what it plans to do next.

levels.headline: Fed expected to hold rates at 27-28 October meeting, with a December hike priced in
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve meets on 27 and 28 October. Traders put only about a 16% chance on a rate rise then, but around 90% on an increase in December, according to CME FedWatch. The Fed raised rates in September to a range of 3.75% to 4%, its first rise since 2023.
US consumer price inflation was 3.7% for the year to September and producer prices were up 6.3%, with energy a key driver. Minutes of the September meeting showed most officials expected another hike by the end of the year without giving a timetable. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has rejected traditional forward guidance and has not signalled the October decision.
A New York Fed survey showed consumers fear price rises over the next year more than at any point since May 2023.
levels.why: US rates influence borrowing costs and markets around the world.

levels.headline: Markets expect the Fed to pause in October and raise in December
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve's next meeting is on 27 and 28 October. Traders see about a 16% chance of a hike then and about 90% for December, according to CME FedWatch. The September increase took rates to 3.75% to 4%, the first since 2023.
Inflation is high: consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September and producer prices 6.3%, largely because of energy. September's minutes showed most officials expected one more hike this year. Chair Kevin Warsh has refused to give forward guidance, and Goldman Sachs reads his comments as pointing to a pause, with a final hike in December.
A New York Fed survey showed inflation fears at their highest since May 2023.
levels.why: Rate decisions in Washington affect the dollar, bond yields and global borrowing.

levels.headline: US Federal Reserve set to hold interest rates, but a rise is expected in December
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve meets on 27 and 28 October. Traders think a rise in interest rates is unlikely then, at about 16%, but they give about a 90% chance of one in December. The Fed raised rates in September to between 3.75% and 4%, the first rise since 2023.
Inflation is high. US consumer prices were up 3.7% in the year to September, mostly because of dearer energy. Most Fed officials expect one more rise this year. The Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, has not given hints about October.
A survey by the New York Fed found people are more worried about rising prices than at any time since May 2023.
levels.why: US interest rates affect borrowing costs around the world.

levels.headline: The US Federal Reserve is expected to wait in October
levels.body:
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, meets on 27 and 28 October. Traders think it will probably leave interest rates alone, with only about a 16% chance of a rise. They think a rise in December is very likely, about 90%.
The Fed raised rates in September to between 3.75% and 4%. That was the first rise since 2023. Prices in the US went up 3.7% in the year to September, mostly because energy costs more. Most Fed officials expect one more rise before the end of the year.
The Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, has not said what will happen. A survey shows people are very worried about rising prices.
levels.why: What the US central bank does affects loans and prices across the world.

levels.headline: The US central bank will probably wait before raising rates again
levels.body:
The US central bank is called the Federal Reserve. It meets on 27 and 28 October. Most traders think it will leave its main interest rate where it is. They think it is more likely to raise it in December.
In September it raised the rate to between 3.75% and 4%. It was the first rise since 2023. Prices in the US are rising fast, at 3.7% a year, mostly because oil and energy cost more. Raising rates makes borrowing cost more, which can slow price rises.
Most officials at the Fed think one more rise is coming this year. The boss, Kevin Warsh, has not said when.
levels.why: What the US does with interest rates can change loan costs everywhere.

levels.headline: The US central bank is expected to wait in October, then raise rates in December
levels.body:
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, meets on 27 and 28 October. Traders think it is unlikely to raise interest rates then, with only about a 16% chance. They think a rise in December is very likely, at about 90%.
The Fed raised its main rate in September to between 3.75% and 4%, the first rise since 2023. Prices in the US went up 3.7% in the year to September, mostly because energy costs more. Raising rates makes borrowing dearer, which can slow price rises.
Most Fed officials expect one more rise this year. The Fed boss, Kevin Warsh, has not said what he will do in October.
levels.why: What the US central bank does can change loan costs in many countries.

levels.headline: The US bank for the whole country will meet soon
levels.body:
The US has a central bank called the Federal Reserve. It sets an interest rate. That is the price of borrowing money. If the rate goes up, loans cost more. Prices in the US are going up fast, at 3.7% a year. So the Fed put the rate up in September.
The Fed meets again on 27 and 28 October. Most traders think it will leave the rate alone this time. They think it will put it up again in December.
The boss of the Fed is Kevin Warsh. He has not said what will happen. Many people are worried about prices.
levels.why: It affects what loans cost in the US and sometimes in other countries.

levels.headline: The US bank may raise the price of borrowing again
levels.body:
The US has a big bank for the whole country called the Federal Reserve. It sets the price of borrowing money, called an interest rate. When prices rise fast, the Fed can make borrowing cost more, so people spend less.
Prices in the US are rising fast, at 3.7% a year, because oil costs more. The Fed already raised its rate in September. It meets again on 27 and 28 October. Most traders think it will wait, and then raise the rate in December.
The boss of the Fed is Kevin Warsh. He has not said what he will do.
levels.why: It affects what loans cost in the US and other countries.

levels.headline: Who sets the price of borrowing in America?
levels.body:
If you borrow a toy from a friend, you give it back. If you borrow money, you give back extra, called interest. In America there is a big bank for the whole country, called the Fed. It decides how much extra people pay.
Prices are going up fast, so the Fed made borrowing cost more in September. That is to slow price rises. The Fed meets again on 27 and 28 October. Most people think it will wait this time. They think it will make borrowing cost more again in December.
The boss of the Fed is called Kevin Warsh.
levels.why: It affects how much people in America pay when they borrow money.

levels.headline: A big bank meets to talk about money
levels.body:
Every country has a big bank that helps look after its money. In America it is called the Fed. It decides how much extra people pay when they borrow, which is called interest.
When things cost more and more, the Fed can make borrowing cost more, so people spend less and prices stop rising so fast. It did this in September. It meets again soon, on 27 and 28 October. Most people think it will wait this time and make borrowing cost more again in December.
The boss is called Kevin Warsh. He has not said what he will do.
levels.why: It affects how much people in America pay when they borrow.

headline: AI stocks slide as neoclouds face credit stress and Solidigm halts IPO review

terms.meaning: A newer firm that rents out computing power for AI.
A kind of insurance against a borrower failing to repay; higher prices signal more worry.
Initial public offering, when a firm first sells shares on a stock market.

levels.headline: AI stocks slide as neoclouds face credit stress and Solidigm halts IPO review
levels.body:
Shares in so-called neocloud firms that rent out computing power for artificial intelligence have fallen sharply. CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have lost at least 30% this month, according to CNBC's report of 24 October. CoreWeave's credit default swap spread has widened past 11%, a level generally seen as distressed, and yields on its 2031 and 2032 unsecured notes have topped 15%.
Morgan Stanley cut its CoreWeave price target to $70 from $99. A Korean neocloud's shares plunged 32% on their trading debut on 20 October, and SK Hynix said Solidigm will halt its review of IPO options, citing market conditions.
Alphabet fell 6% last week ahead of its third-quarter results, and analysts question Nvidia's role as a financier of the AI buildout.
levels.why: Heavy AI spending on borrowed money is now being tested by investors.

levels.headline: AI buildout hit by neocloud sell-off and rising credit worries
levels.body:
Neocloud stocks, which rent out AI computing power, led a broad AI-related sell-off. CNBC reports that CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are each down at least 30% this month. CoreWeave's credit default swap spread is above 11%, generally viewed as distressed, and its 2031 and 2032 notes yield over 15%.
Morgan Stanley cut its CoreWeave target to $70 from $99. A Korean neocloud IPO fell 32% on debut on 20 October, and SK Hynix said Solidigm would stop reviewing IPO options, citing volatility and a semiconductor correction.
Alphabet dropped 6% ahead of earnings. Gartner forecasts that over 80% of neocloud providers will cease independent operations by 2030.
levels.why: It shows doubts about whether AI spending will earn its money back.

levels.headline: Shares in AI computing firms fall sharply amid debt worries
levels.body:
Shares in neocloud firms, which rent out computing power for artificial intelligence, have fallen sharply. CNBC says CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have each lost at least 30% this month. Investors now see CoreWeave's debt as risky: insurance against it failing to repay has become very expensive, and its bonds pay over 15%.
Morgan Stanley lowered its price target for CoreWeave. A Korean firm's shares fell 32% on their first day of trading on 20 October, and the chipmaker SK Hynix said its unit Solidigm will stop reviewing a share sale because of market conditions.
Alphabet's shares fell 6% before its results. Gartner expects most neocloud firms to stop operating independently by 2030.
levels.why: AI firms rely on borrowing, so investor doubt can spread.

levels.headline: AI computing companies lose a third of their value as debt fears grow
levels.body:

levels.headline: AI company shares drop as people worry about debt
levels.body:
Artificial intelligence, or AI, needs very powerful computers. Some firms rent them out. They are called neoclouds. Their shares have dropped a lot this month. Three of them have each lost nearly a third of their value or more.
One reason is debt. These firms borrowed lots of money to buy computers. Now lenders worry they might not be able to pay it back, so they ask for more interest. A big bank also lowered its target for one firm's share price. A new firm in Korea lost a third of its value on day one.
Many people are now asking if AI will make enough money.
levels.why: It shows how risky it can be to borrow lots of money for a big idea.

levels.headline: Shares in AI computer firms are falling
levels.body:
Artificial intelligence, or AI, is a way to make computers that can do clever things. It needs lots of powerful computers, which are expensive. Some firms rent them out. Their shares have dropped by a third or more this month.
These firms borrowed lots of money to buy the computers. Now the people who lent the money feel nervous. They want to be paid extra to take the risk. A big bank has said one of the firms might be worth less than it thought.
Many people are asking if AI will make enough money to pay for all this.
levels.why: It shows how risky it can be to borrow a lot for a big idea.

levels.headline: Worry about a big, costly idea
levels.body:
Imagine a group of children borrow lots of pocket money to build a giant sandcastle. They hope people will pay to visit it. But then the tide looks like it might come in, and the people who lent the money get worried.
Something like that is happening with artificial intelligence, or AI. Firms borrowed lots of money to buy super-powerful computers. This month, their shares have dropped by a third or more. People are not sure if enough customers will pay to use them.
The people who lent the money want extra for taking a risk.
levels.why: It shows that big ideas can be risky if you borrow a lot.

levels.headline: A very big idea is worrying some grown-ups
levels.body:
Some companies are building super-powerful computers for something called AI. It lets computers do clever things like write and draw. Building them costs a huge amount of money, and the companies borrowed a lot of it.
This month, the price of their shares has dropped a lot. It is a bit like a stall at a school fair where the sweets are suddenly worth less. People who lent the money are worried they might not get it back, so they ask for more in return.
Nobody knows yet if the big idea will work out.
levels.why: It shows that big ideas can be risky if you borrow a lot.
